question: A 38-year-old woman undergoes a diagnostic hysteroscopy for a 6-month history of small volume intermenstrual bleeding with no other complaints. There is no history of pelvic pain, painful intercourse, or vaginal discharge other than blood. During the procedure, a red beefy pedunculated mass is seen arising from the endometrium of the anterior wall of the uterus that has well-demarcated borders. This mass is resected and sent for histopathological examination. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Red beefy pedunculated mass arising from endometrium" -> "Well-demarcated borders" -> "Most likely diagnosis is endometrial polyp" -> 95%

CHAIN: "Small volume intermenstrual bleeding" -> "No other complaints" -> "No history of pelvic pain, painful intercourse, or vaginal discharge other than blood" -> "Red beefy pedunculated mass seen during hysteroscopy" -> "Well-demarcated borders" -> "Most likely diagnosis is endometrial polyp" -> 90%
enhanced_information: The most likely diagnosis for the red beefy pedunculated mass with well-demarcated borders arising from the endometrium in a 38-year-old woman with small volume intermenstrual bleeding is an endometrial polyp. This conclusion is supported by the clinical presentation and characteristics observed during hysteroscopy.
analysis: The core medical principle here is to consider the clinical presentation and characteristics observed during the hysteroscopy. In this case, the red beefy pedunculated mass with well-demarcated borders arising from the endometrium in a 38-year-old woman with intermenstrual bleeding is most likely indicative of an endometrial polyp. Endometrial polyps are a common cause of abnormal uterine bleeding and are characterized by their appearance during hysteroscopy. The absence of other significant symptoms like pelvic pain, painful intercourse, or discharge also supports this diagnosis.
